title: Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019
short_title: Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would extend income management programs and transition participants in certain regions onto a cashless debit card trial.
It would set end dates for the card trials, remove participant caps, and add the Northern Territory and Cape York as trial areas.
The changes would also let people in the Bundaberg and Hervey Bay region join the trial voluntarily and improve how the evaluation works.
changes: Extends the end date of the income management program to 30 June 2021 and sets the Cape York cashless debit card trial end date as 31 December 2021.
Removes the upper limit on how many people can be in the cashless debit card trial.
Allows residents of the Bundaberg and Hervey Bay trial site to choose to participate in the cashless debit card trial.
Names the Northern Territory and Cape York as cashless debit card trial areas and moves income management participants there onto the card trial in 2020.
Permits the Secretary to tell a community body when someone leaves the cashless debit card trial.
Makes the evaluation process easier to run.
summary.affected: People receiving income management payments in the Northern Territory, Cape York, and the Bundaberg and Hervey Bay region, as well as the Secretary and community bodies.

speeches.speaker: Stuart Robert
speeches.brief: The Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019 transitions approximately 23,000 welfare recipients in the Northern Territory and Cape York from the BasicsCard to the cashless debit card, with the transition occurring community-by-community over nine months from 1 April 2020 and backed by almost $18 million in support. The bill also extends the cashless debit card across all four current trial sites until 30 June 2021, arguing the card provides greater consumer choice, reduces social harm, and has shown positive results such as decreases in drug and alcohol issues and crime.

speeches.speaker: Linda Burney
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019, arguing it is discriminatory, lacks evidence of effectiveness, and would not create jobs, while announcing Labor would seek to amend the bill in the Senate to make the cashless debit card voluntary in the Northern Territory unless a community requests it or individual circumstances apply.

speeches.speaker: Jason Falinski
speeches.brief: The government is continuing the rollout of the cashless debit card, citing reduced violence, drug and alcohol issues, and improved child health and financial management, and supports the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019 as part of the solution.

speeches.speaker: Mike Freelander
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019, arguing it is discriminatory, lacks evidence, and would disproportionately affect First Nations Australians (80% of those on income management in the Northern Territory). The speaker called for the cashless debit card to be voluntary, supported by community consultation and wraparound services, and cited research showing a 100-gram drop in birth weights among affected populations.

speeches.speaker: Kate Thwaites
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019, arguing it is discriminatory and disproportionately impacts Indigenous Australians. They noted over 80% of the 23,000 people on income management in the Northern Territory are Indigenous, cited no evidence the cashless debit card works, and highlighted that communities like Milingimbi were not consulted.

speeches.speaker: Joanne Ryan
speeches.brief: The opposition opposed the bill to transition income management to a cashless debit card, arguing it is a failed, short-term solution that is discriminatory against Indigenous Australians and lacks evidence of effectiveness. They highlighted that 80% of Northern Territory recipients are Indigenous, cited research showing no improvement in child health outcomes, and called for voluntary, community-consulted programs with wraparound support instead.

speeches.speaker: Andrew Wilkie
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019, arguing the cashless debit card expansion unfairly punishes community members who do not drink, smoke, gamble or use drugs.

speeches.speaker: Rebekha Sharkie
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that cashless debit card trial results are mixed and lack conclusive academic evidence, and called for delaying the bill until the University of Adelaide report is released and genuine consultation is conducted with affected remote Aboriginal communities, particularly in the Northern Territory.

speeches.speaker: Stuart Robert
speeches.brief: The government argued the bill extends the cashless debit card trial to 30 June 2021, transitions income management participants in the Northern Territory and Cape York to the card, and limits the ministerial power to vary the restriction rate to a maximum of 80%, while removing compulsory participation for age pensioners except in Cape York.

speeches.speaker: Warren Snowdon
speeches.brief: The speaker opposed the Social Security (Administration) Amendment (Income Management to Cashless Debit Card Transition) Bill 2019 and its amendments, arguing the government imposed the policy without consulting Aboriginal people in the Northern Territory. They stated the BasicsCard was already harmful, cited effective alcohol measures like floor pricing and police enforcement as alternatives, and called the blanket approach disrespectful and undemocratic.
